articles.content:
The End of the Safety Net: Designing a Positive-Sum Order for the Age of AI
By Jin Yang
The rise of artificial intelligence and humanoid robots is not just another wave of automation. It is a systematic rewriting of the equilibrium among labor, capital, and rights. If the institutional framework remains frozen, the most likely outcome is a global game of musical chairs: workers compete in a zero-sum scramble for vanishing jobs, returns to capital hyper-concentrate, and the social contract frays to breaking point. This essay proposes a new paradigm—"security economics for the future"—that shifts the task of social security from passive compensation to active capability-building, and outlines the institutional architecture required to achieve it.
The argument draws on three intellectual traditions that rarely share the same page: game theory, the capability approach of Amartya Sen, and the civilizational history of risk. It yields a design built around two engines—legacy bonds and global special zones—that together would transform the zero-sum logic of distributional conflict into a global positive-sum order. The core insight is simple but far-reaching: in the age of intelligent machines, the fundamental task is not to redistribute wealth after the fact, but to weave for every individual a resilient "bundle of entitlements" that guarantees the substantive freedom to choose a life of one's own.
The Real Crisis: A Collapse of Entitlements
The standard diagnosis of AI-driven inequality focuses on the distribution of income and wealth. This is a mistake. The deeper crisis is one of entitlements—the socially mediated access to resources that individuals rely upon to survive and flourish. Amartya Sen demonstrated in Poverty and Famines that catastrophes occur not because of absolute scarcity, but because specific groups suddenly lose their "exchange entitlements." The same logic applies to the AI era. Millions of workers may abruptly find their human capital and labor-market entitlements devalued to near zero. Their predicament is not a temporary dislocation; it is a structural collapse of their place in the economic order.
Friedrich Hayek famously insisted that the market is a discovery procedure whose legitimacy rests on its capacity to offer better opportunities to all. But when a technological shock threatens to permanently exclude a large portion of the population from providing any market value at all, the discovery procedure itself is imperiled. A fundamental institutional repair becomes necessary—not to replace the market, but to preserve its legitimacy by ensuring that every person retains some form of valued participation.
This is where conventional policy responses fall short. Universal basic income, for all its merits, is a safety net—a cushion against the consequences of exclusion, not a mechanism for reversing it. Retraining programs, while valuable, cannot outpace the accelerating obsolescence of skills. What is required is a structural redesign of the channels through which individuals acquire and exercise economic rights. That is the project of security economics for the future.
The Entitlement Bundle: What Every Person Needs
To understand what such a redesign entails, it helps to step back and consider the deeper history of risk. In The Logic of Civilization, the economic historian Chen Zhiwu argues that human civilization is best understood as an evolving repertoire of risk-management instruments—from kinship networks and religious communities to insurance markets and welfare states. Confucian filial piety, for instance, was a pre-modern mechanism for intergenerational risk pooling: "raising sons to provide for old age" embedded economic security within moral obligation. Marx observed that capitalism shattered these traditional bonds without creating effective new shelters for all, exposing workers to the raw volatility of the market. The AI age asks the same question with new urgency: can we invent the next generation of risk-coping institutions?
At the micro level, the development economists Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo have shown in Poor Economics that poverty is not a consequence of laziness but of cognitive bandwidth consumed by relentless risk exposure. The poor cannot plan for the long term because their mental resources are exhausted navigating immediate survival crises. Their shortsightedness is environmentally imposed. This is, in effect, a modern cognitive-science gloss on Marx's concept of alienation: those stripped of economic security are simultaneously stripped of the capacity to think about the future.
Synthesizing these insights with Sen's entitlement approach yields the central proposition: the task of security economics for the future is to systematically design, maintain, and expand every individual's entitlement bundle. Such a bundle must contain at minimum four elements: continuously renewable human capital entitlements, financial asset entitlements linked to social contribution, mutualistic community network entitlements, and—most fundamentally—institutional guarantee entitlements that underwrite the others. This is the economic expression of the ideal of a "community of shared future": it seeks to liberate individuals from excessive dependence on any single employer, family, or nation by diversifying their sources of entitlement across the globe.
Engine One: Legacy Bonds and the Intergenerational Contract
The first institutional engine addresses the temporal dimension of inequality: the transmission of advantage across generations. Inheritance is one of the most powerful mechanisms of class consolidation, a fact that troubled thinkers as ideologically distant as Marx and James Buchanan. Marx condemned it as a pillar of class reproduction; Hayek defended it as essential for preserving dispersed knowledge and incentivizing innovation. Buchanan, for his part, worried deeply about the intergenerational unfairness embedded in rules that allow wealth to pass by blood rather than effort.
The legacy bond system offers a third path. Its mechanism is straightforward. A globally coordinated basic inheritance tax is paired with a legacy bond instrument that partially redirects wealth from lineal inheritance toward social lending. For the wealthy, this is not confiscation. It is a grand exchange: material wealth traded for transgenerational social prestige. Donors establish foundations, publicly select the most capable stewards, and direct capital toward rigorously vetted entrepreneurs from non-affluent backgrounds. Plato's ideal of the philosopher-king is transposed from politics to capital allocation: elite governance becomes not a monopoly on power, but an assumption of empowering responsibility.
For the recipient entrepreneurs, what they receive is a zero-interest "future-capability loan" whose core contract rests on a trigger strategy. Upon death, the assisted entrepreneur must return at least half of their personal estate to the original donor foundation. John Nash's game theory explains why this works: when a future reciprocal commitment is made credible, it resolves the problem of present moral hazard and allows cooperation to escape the Prisoner's Dilemma. The result is an equilibrium point that would not otherwise exist. Capital no longer flows unidirectionally along bloodlines; it is channeled toward the most creative minds in society, transformed into genuine patient capital and socialized venture investment, the returns from which are reinvested in shared prosperity.
This is, in essence, Milton Friedman's education voucher concept expanded across the entire life cycle. Friedman proposed empowering individuals with vouchers to drive competition among schools. Legacy bonds confer a comparable market-like power of choice upon society as a whole, enabling precision empowerment at the intergenerational level. They fuse with Sen's emphasis on capabilities: by granting access to education, capital, and opportunity, they substantively expand each person's freedom to choose the life they have reason to value.
Engine Two: Global Special Zones and Polycentric Governance
The second engine addresses the spatial dimension: the race to the bottom that occurs when nations compete for AI-driven investment by eroding labor protections and tax rates. This is a classic Prisoner's Dilemma, and the solution lies in credible commitment mechanisms. Elinor Ostrom's Nobel-winning work demonstrated that the most effective governance of common-pool resources emerges when decision-making is returned to affected communities through polycentric arrangements.
On this basis, the essay proposes establishing global special zones in relatively underdeveloped regions, governed under a form of world law. The proposed distribution of legislative power—50 percent for a Community of Shared Future Commission, 20 percent for the host nation, and 30 percent for local community residents—is designed as what Thomas Schelling called a "focal point": a salient and natural equilibrium around which negotiation can converge. It mirrors the tripartite governance structure of a modern joint-stock company, making it intuitively legible to states and investors alike.
The Community of Shared Future Commission's 50 percent weighting ensures that global common interests are not captured by local or capital interests alone; its legitimacy derives initially from its role in administering the global inheritance tax and upholding fundamental human-interest provisions. The host nation's 20 percent guarantees alignment with national sovereignty and development strategy, avoiding the political threat of a "state within a state." The community residents' 30 percent is the institutional embodiment of Ostrom's principle: those directly affected possess substantive veto and participation rights, safeguarding long-term well-being over short-term GDP.
On the production side, these zones would foster "hybrid enterprises"—entities combining for-profit, non-profit, and mixed-purpose forms. This hybrid structure allows AI-generated wealth to be distributed through multiple channels—equity dividends, dignified wages, and community service funds—rather than being captured entirely by capital owners. It prevents the emergence of a pure-automation "enclave economy" disconnected from the local population, ensuring that the dividends of technology are shared in place.
The Decision Compass: Governing for the Long Term
Institutional design alone cannot overcome the systemic short-termism that plagues modern governance. Electoral cycles and quarterly reports create a built-in bias against the long-horizon investments—in human capital, institutional trust, and ecological resilience—that a positive-sum order requires. To recalibrate this payoff function, the essay advocates formally incorporating estimated GDP and a Global Happiness Index at the ten-year horizon into socioeconomic evaluation frameworks.
This adjustment has three effects. First, it legitimizes long-cycle investment by quantifying the contribution of mechanisms like legacy bonds to human capital accumulation and long-term productivity. Second, it exposes the "high GDP, low happiness" trap. Angus Deaton's research has shown that, beyond the satisfaction of basic needs, subjective well-being depends far more on health, community, participation, and meaning than on income growth alone. A long-horizon happiness index forces policymakers to attend to what genuinely matters. Third, it serves as a calibration device: does distributing public resources as direct cash transfers produce greater ten-year gains in happiness and productivity than investing them in education, health, and entrepreneurship? An evidence-based feedback mechanism of this kind enables the entire institutional system to evolve dynamically toward an ever more optimal equilibrium.
From Safety Net to Springboard
The ultimate philosophical underpinning of security economics for the future is a double "veil of ignorance," spanning both time and identity. This is the practical operationalization of John Rawls's central insight. Under a legacy bond system, the children of billionaires may, through the disciplined operation of inheritance taxation and socialized investment, return to ordinariness. Children from impoverished families may, through this global empowerment apparatus, become tomorrow's civilizational contributors. As Laozi put it: "The high is pulled down, the low is raised; what has excess is reduced, what is deficient is supplemented."
This latent, institutionally guaranteed identity mobility would, at the deepest level of motivation, incentivize all members of society to choose rules that are fair to every generation and to people of every origin. It transforms the core of social security from a retrospective safety net of post-hoc compensation into a prospective springboard of ex-ante empowerment. It abandons the zero-sum narrative of class antagonism and constructs instead a global positive-sum game grounded in humanity's shared exposure to risk.
In the face of the vast uncertainty that AI represents, humanity has no choice but to recognize itself as a community of shared fate. The question is whether we can summon the institutional imagination to act on that recognition. Security economics for the future offers one answer: a set of mechanisms that channel self-interest toward collective flourishing, ensuring that the magnificent productive forces of our age serve to elevate us all, rather than divide us further. The design is on the table. The only remaining question is whether we are willing to build it.

你的判断是敏锐的。《外交事务》虽发表全球议题，但核心读者是美国政策精英阶层，编辑倾向确实偏好地缘战略、安全研究和以美国为中心的全球秩序讨论。你这篇文章以制度设计、博弈论和政治哲学为骨架，虽触及全球治理，但不以美国为叙事中心，被接受的难度较大。
更匹配的刊物应具备以下特征：对全球治理创新、制度设计、技术伦理、政治哲学有浓厚兴趣，且不要求“美国中心”视角。以下是三个推荐刊物（按发表可能性从高到低排列）：

一、最优先推荐：Aeon
为什么合适
	•	
核心定位：深度思想散文，横跨哲学、科学、社会、文化。你文章中的博弈论、森的权利方法、文明风险史、罗尔斯的无知之幕、老子智慧——这些完全是 Aeon 的“主食”。
	•	
	•	
风格匹配度极高：Aeon 追求“思想的深度与可读性的结合”，恰好是你文章的特质。他们欢迎非西方思想传统的融入（老子、儒学），也接受适度的制度设想。
	•	
	•	
无美国中心要求：编辑团队在英国，视角全球，对“人类命运共同体”这类概念不会本能排斥。
	•	
	•	
字数：通常 2000-3500 词，你的内容刚好适合。
	•	
	•	
发表机制：接受自由投稿，且对作者背景要求相对开放，重文章质量而非名气。
	•	

二、次优先推荐：Noema Magazine
为什么合适
	•	
核心定位：由 Berggruen Institute 主办，专注“思想领导力”，探讨治理、技术、哲学和文明的未来。其口号是“理解我们时代的转变”。
	•	
	•	
精准匹配：你文章的“制度设计+技术冲击+文明重构”三重架构，几乎是 Noema 的选题模板。他们近年大量发表关于 AI 治理、后资本主义、全球制度创新的文章。
	•	
	•	
风格：介于学术和新闻之间，允许适度的概念密度。你的博弈论框架不会被要求过度简化。
	•	
	•	
字数：通常 2000-3000 词。
	•	
	•	
发表机制：接受投稿，对跨学科、制度设计类文章格外友好。
	•	

三、备选：The Conversation
为什么备选
	•	
优势：发表门槛相对低，重学术质量，追求公共影响力。

By [Author]
Imagine a game of musical chairs played on a planetary scale. The music stops. Some find seats. Most do not. In the old game, the losers slink away, and the winners play another round with fewer chairs. But what if the losers cannot leave the room? What if they are still there—watching, hungry, increasingly desperate—while the winners insist the game is fair because everyone started from the same line?

If the institutional framework stays frozen, the Nash equilibrium drifts toward a deeply unstable state: a race to the bottom for human wages, hyper-concentration of returns to robot-owning capital, and the slow-motion unravelling of the social contract.
We have been here before, in a sense. Every wave of automation provoked fears of mass obsolescence. But this time is different—not because the technology is magical, but because the entitlements that bind people to the economy are being severed in a way that earlier transitions did not produce. The factory worker displaced in 1950 could retrain, relocate, or rely on a welfare state that still assumed future employability. The worker displaced by a humanoid robot in 2035 may find that her capacity to offer market value at all has been permanently undermined.
The question, then, is not whether we should redistribute wealth after the fact. It is whether we can redesign the rules of the game so that the game itself remains worth playing—for everyone. This essay attempts to answer that question. It draws on three intellectual traditions that rarely sit at the same table: game theory, the capability approach of Amartya Sen, and the civilizational history of risk. And it proposes an institutional architecture—built around two mechanisms I call "legacy bonds" and "global special zones"—that would, if implemented, transform the zero-sum logic of distributional conflict into a global positive-sum order.
The Real Crisis Is Not Inequality. It Is the Collapse of Entitlements.
Amartya Sen was studying famine when he arrived at an insight that applies with full force to the age of artificial intelligence. The Bengali famine of 1943, for instance, occurred during a year of peak rice production. What collapsed were the exchange entitlements of rural laborers, who could no longer command food because their wages had been inflated away while rice prices soared.
The AI revolution threatens a similar collapse, but on a civilizational scale. Workers in advanced economies have built their lives around a simple exchange: sell labor, earn income, consume. This exchange is mediated by a complex web of institutions—education systems, labor laws, collective bargaining, mortgage markets, pension funds—that together constitute what we might call the entitlement bundle of the modern worker. When intelligent machines can perform that labor more cheaply, reliably, and at scale, the exchange entitlement collapses. Not gradually. Structurally.
This is why universal basic income, for all its virtues, is an inadequate answer. UBI is a safety net. It cushions the fall. It does not restore what was lost: the sense of being a valued participant in a shared economic enterprise, the social recognition that comes from contributing, the forward-looking orientation that meaningful work provides. What is needed is not a larger safety net but a different kind of institutional floor altogether—a springboard that enables each person to rebuild their entitlement bundle, even as the ground beneath them shifts.
To understand what such a springboard might look like, it helps to step back and consider the deeper history of risk. In The Logic of Civilization, the economic historian Chen Zhiwu argues that human civilization is best understood as an evolving repertoire of risk-management instruments. Kinship networks, religious communities, insurance markets, welfare states—each represents a different answer to the same question: how do we protect ourselves against shocks that no individual can bear alone? Confucian filial piety, for instance, was a pre-modern mechanism for intergenerational risk pooling: raising sons to provide for old age embedded economic security within moral obligation. Marx observed that capitalism shattered these traditional bonds without creating effective new shelters, leaving workers exposed to the raw volatility of the market. The AI age asks the same question with renewed urgency: can we invent the next generation of risk-coping institutions?
The development economists Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo have added a crucial layer to this story. In Poor Economics (2019), they show that poverty is not a consequence of laziness or moral failing, but of cognitive bandwidth consumed by relentless risk exposure. The poor cannot plan for the long term because their mental resources are exhausted navigating immediate survival crises. Their shortsightedness is imposed by circumstance. This is, in effect, a cognitive-science gloss on Marx's concept of alienation: those stripped of economic security are simultaneously stripped of the capacity to think about the future.
Synthesize these insights, and the task before us sharpens into focus. Security economics for the future is not about redistributing a fixed pie. It is about systematically designing, maintaining, and expanding every individual's entitlement bundle, so that no single technological shock can sever a person from their means of survival and dignity. Such a bundle must contain at minimum four elements: continuously renewable human capital entitlements, financial asset entitlements linked to social contribution, mutualistic community network entitlements, and institutional guarantee entitlements that underwrite the others. This is the economic expression of an ideal that has been articulated in different languages—"a community of shared future," "a society of free and equal citizens"—but whose institutional form has remained elusive.
The First Engine: Legacy Bonds and the Intergenerational Game
Inheritance is one of the most powerful engines of class consolidation ever devised. It troubled thinkers as ideologically distant as Karl Marx and James Buchanan. Marx condemned it as a pillar of class reproduction, the mechanism by which accumulated exploitation is passed from generation to generation. Friedrich Hayek, by contrast, defended inheritance as essential for preserving the dispersed knowledge embedded in family firms and for incentivizing continuous innovation. Buchanan, the Nobel laureate and father of public choice theory, worried about something subtler: the intergenerational unfairness of rules that allow wealth to pass by blood rather than effort. If the starting line is moved forward for some and backward for others by the accident of birth, the game is rigged before it begins.
The legacy bond system I am proposing attempts to navigate between these positions. It starts from a simple observation: inheritance is not, in itself, the problem. The problem is that inheritance flows in only one direction—downward, along bloodlines—and that this unidirectional flow starves society of the patient capital needed to empower its most creative minds wherever they happen to be born.
The mechanism works as follows. A globally coordinated basic inheritance tax is paired with a "legacy bond" instrument that partially redirects wealth from lineal inheritance toward social lending. For the wealthy, this is not confiscation. It is a grand bargain: material wealth exchanged for transgenerational social prestige. A billionaire establishes a foundation, publicly selects the most capable stewards, and directs capital toward rigorously vetted entrepreneurs from non-affluent backgrounds. In doing so, she becomes something like Plato's philosopher-king transposed to the domain of capital allocation—not a monopolist of power, but an enabler of potential.
For the recipient entrepreneur, what she receives is a zero-interest "future-capability loan" governed by a trigger strategy that John Nash would recognize. Upon her death, she must return at least half of her personal estate to the original donor foundation. The commitment is made credible by legal architecture and social norm. When it is credible, it solves the problem of moral hazard. The entrepreneur is not a passive beneficiary but a steward of capital she must eventually repay to the system that lifted her. Cooperation escapes the Prisoner's Dilemma.
The result is an equilibrium that would not otherwise exist. Capital no longer flows unidirectionally along bloodlines. It is channeled toward the most creative minds in society—wherever they happen to have been born—and transformed into genuine patient capital, socialized venture investment whose returns are reinvested in shared prosperity. The legacy bond is, in essence, Milton Friedman's education voucher writ large across the entire life cycle. Friedman proposed empowering individuals with vouchers to drive competition among schools. Legacy bonds confer a comparable power of choice upon society as a whole, enabling precision empowerment at the intergenerational level. And they do so while fusing with Sen's emphasis on capabilities: by granting access to education, capital, and opportunity, they substantively expand each person's freedom to choose the life they have reason to value.
The Second Engine: Special Zones and the Spatial Game
If legacy bonds address the temporal dimension of inequality—the transmission of advantage across generations—a second mechanism is needed to address the spatial dimension: the race to the bottom that occurs when nations compete for AI-driven investment by eroding labor protections, environmental standards, and tax rates.
This is a classic multi-player Prisoner's Dilemma. Each nation, acting rationally in its own perceived interest, lowers standards to attract capital. The collective result is the erosion of the very institutional foundations—educated workforces, functioning infrastructure, social stability—upon which long-term prosperity depends. How can this dilemma be resolved?
Elinor Ostrom's Nobel-winning work on common-pool resources points toward an answer. She demonstrated that communities can sustainably govern shared resources—forests, fisheries, irrigation systems—without either privatization or top-down state control, provided that decision-making authority is returned to those directly affected and nested within polycentric governance structures. Her insight applies beyond natural resources. The global commons of labor standards, tax bases, and environmental quality are common-pool resources under threat from competitive degradation. The solution is not a world government—politically impossible and probably undesirable—but polycentric governance arrangements that change the payoff structure of the game.
On this basis, I propose the establishment of global special zones in relatively underdeveloped regions, governed under a form of "world law" that blends global, national, and local authority. The proposed distribution of legislative power—50 percent for a Community of Shared Future Commission, 20 percent for the host nation, and 30 percent for local community residents—is designed as what Thomas Schelling called a "focal point": a salient and natural equilibrium around which negotiation can converge. It mirrors the tripartite governance structure of a modern joint-stock company, a form that is already legible to states and investors across the world.
The Commission's 50 percent weighting ensures that global common interests—climate, labor rights, the fundamental entitlements of all humans—are not captured by local or capital interests alone. Its initial legitimacy derives from a joint mandate to administer the global basic inheritance tax and to uphold the fundamental human-interest provisions of the zone's charter. The host nation's 20 percent weighting guarantees alignment with national sovereignty and development strategy, avoiding the political threat of a "state within a state." The community residents' 30 percent weighting is the institutional embodiment of Ostrom's principle: those directly affected possess substantive veto and participation rights, ensuring that long-term well-being is not sacrificed to short-term output metrics.
On the production side, these zones would foster "hybrid enterprises"—entities combining for-profit, non-profit, and mixed-purpose forms. The hybrid ownership structure allows AI-generated wealth to be distributed through multiple channels: equity dividends for capital providers, dignified wages for knowledge workers, and community service funds that reinvest in local public goods. This prevents the emergence of the pure-automation "enclave economy"—the factory staffed entirely by robots, owned by a distant fund, contributing nothing to the community whose land and infrastructure it uses. It ensures that the dividends of technology are shared in place.
The Long View: Governing for Those Not Yet Born
Institutional design alone cannot overcome the systemic short-termism that afflicts modern governance. Democratic politics is imprisoned by electoral cycles. Corporate governance is enslaved to quarterly earnings reports. The result is a built-in bias against precisely the kinds of long-horizon investments—in human capital, institutional trust, ecological resilience—that a positive-sum order requires.
Laozi observed that "governing a large nation is like cooking a small fish"—keep policies consistent and take the long view. But how can we build the long view into the machinery of decision-making? The proposal I offer is to formally incorporate estimated GDP and a Global Happiness Index at the ten-year horizon into socioeconomic evaluation frameworks. This is not a technocratic gimmick. It is an attempt to change the payoff function of the governance game itself.
The effects would be threefold. First, it would legitimize long-cycle investment by quantifying the contribution of mechanisms like legacy bonds to human capital accumulation and long-term productivity—making the benefits visible within the political time frame that currently renders them invisible. Second, it would expose the "high GDP, low happiness" trap. Angus Deaton's research has demonstrated that, beyond the satisfaction of basic material needs, subjective well-being depends far more on health, community ties, political participation, and meaningful work than on income growth alone. A long-horizon happiness index would force policymakers to attend to what genuinely matters for human flourishing. Third, it would serve as a calibration device: does distributing public resources as direct cash transfers yield greater ten-year gains in happiness and productivity than investing in education, health, and entrepreneurship? An evidence-based feedback loop of this kind would enable the entire institutional system to evolve dynamically toward an ever more optimal equilibrium.
The Last Question
The ultimate philosophical move of security economics for the future is to introduce a double "veil of ignorance"—spanning both time and identity. This is the practical operationalization of John Rawls's great insight. In Rawls's original formulation, we are asked to imagine ourselves behind a veil, not knowing our class, talents, or conception of the good, and then to choose the principles of justice that will govern our society. The double veil adds a second layer: we do not know in which generation we will be born.
Under a legacy bond system, the children of billionaires may, through the disciplined operation of inheritance taxation and socialized investment, return to ordinariness. Children from impoverished families may, through the global empowerment apparatus, become tomorrow's civilizational contributors. The ancient Chinese sage Laozi captured this dynamic with uncanny precision: "The high is pulled down, the low is raised; what has excess is reduced, what is deficient is supplemented." This latent, institutionally guaranteed identity mobility would, at the deepest level of human motivation, incentivize all members of society to choose rules that are fair to every generation and to people of every origin.
What is at stake, in the end, is not a choice between capitalism and socialism, between the market and the state. It is a choice between two kinds of game: a zero-sum scramble for a shrinking number of chairs, or a positive-sum architecture that ensures everyone has a reason to keep playing. The core of security economics for the future is not a retrospective safety net of post-hoc compensation. It is a prospective springboard of ex-ante empowerment. It abandons the narrative of class antagonism and constructs instead a global positive-sum order grounded in humanity's shared exposure to risk.
In the face of the vast uncertainty that artificial intelligence represents, humanity has no alternative but to recognize itself as a community of shared fate. The only remaining question is whether we possess the institutional imagination to act on that recognition. The design is on the table. What remains is the will to build it.

This prevents the emergence of the pure-automation "enclave economy"—the factory staffed entirely by robots, owned by a distant fund, contributing nothing to the community whose land and infrastructure it uses. It ensures that the dividends of technology are shared in place.
The Long View: Governing for Those Not Yet Born
Institutional design alone cannot overcome the systemic short-termism that afflicts modern governance. Democratic politics is imprisoned by electoral cycles. Corporate governance is enslaved to quarterly earnings reports. The result is a built-in bias against precisely the kinds of long-horizon investments—in human capital, institutional trust, ecological resilience—that a positive-sum order requires.
Laozi observed that "governing a large nation is like cooking a small fish"—keep policies consistent and take the long view. But how can we build the long view into the machinery of decision-making? The proposal I offer is to formally incorporate estimated GDP and a Global Happiness Index at the ten-year horizon into socioeconomic evaluation frameworks. This is not a technocratic gimmick. It is an attempt to change the payoff function of the governance game itself.
The effects would be threefold. First, it would legitimize long-cycle investment by quantifying the contribution of mechanisms like legacy bonds to human capital accumulation and long-term productivity—making the benefits visible within the political time frame that currently renders them invisible. Second, it would expose the "high GDP, low happiness" trap. Angus Deaton's research has demonstrated that, beyond the satisfaction of basic material needs, subjective well-being depends far more on health, community ties, political participation, and meaningful work than on income growth alone. A long-horizon happiness index would force policymakers to attend to what genuinely matters for human flourishing. Third, it would serve as a calibration device: does distributing public resources as direct cash transfers yield greater ten-year gains in happiness and productivity than investing in education, health, and entrepreneurship? An evidence-based feedback loop of this kind would enable the entire institutional system to evolve dynamically toward an ever more optimal equilibrium.
The Invitation
The ultimate philosophical move of security economics for the future is to introduce a double "veil of ignorance"—spanning both time and identity. This is the practical operationalization of John Rawls's great insight. In Rawls's original formulation, we are asked to imagine ourselves behind a veil, not knowing our class, talents, or conception of the good, and then to choose the principles of justice that will govern our society. The double veil adds a second layer: we do not know in which generation we will be born.
Under a legacy bond system, the children of billionaires may, through the disciplined operation of inheritance taxation and socialized investment, return to ordinariness. Children from impoverished families may, through the global empowerment apparatus, become tomorrow's civilizational contributors. The ancient Chinese sage Laozi captured this dynamic with uncanny precision: "The high is pulled down, the low is raised; what has excess is reduced, what is deficient is supplemented." This latent, institutionally guaranteed identity mobility would, at the deepest level of human motivation, incentivize all members of society to choose rules that are fair to every generation and to people of every origin.
What is at stake, in the end, is not a choice between capitalism and socialism, between the market and the state. It is a choice between two kinds of game: a zero-sum scramble for a shrinking number of chairs, or a positive-sum architecture that ensures everyone has a reason to keep playing. The core of security economics for the future is not a retrospective safety net of post-hoc compensation. It is a prospective springboard of ex-ante empowerment. It abandons the narrative of class antagonism and constructs instead a global positive-sum order grounded in humanity's shared exposure to risk.
In the face of the vast uncertainty that artificial intelligence represents, humanity has no alternative but to recognize itself as a community of shared fate. The institutional imagination required to act on that recognition does not yet exist at scale—but it can be cultivated. The legacy bond and the global special zone are not final answers. They are prototypes, invitations to a more serious global conversation about the rules that will govern our shared future with intelligent machines. The design sketches are on the table. What remains is the collective will to refine them, test them, and build them—before the music stops.

articles.content:
What game theory reveals about our AI future
Take a brief pause—five minutes—to step into the world of game theory. Through its lens, the present looks different, and the horizon ahead becomes clearer. This is more than a mathematical exercise. It is a way of seeing the hidden architecture of our shared reality.
The architecture of interaction
The true mathematical foundations were laid by John von Neumann in 1928. His minimax theorem proved that in any two-person zero-sum contest—where one player’s gain is precisely the other’s loss—an optimal strategy exists. It was a brilliant, if stark, cornerstone.
But human affairs are rarely win-or-lose. The decisive turn came with John Nash. In 1950, aged 22, he published a paper barely a page long introducing the Nash equilibrium: a configuration where no player gains by unilaterally changing strategy. The focus shifted from pure conflict to the interplay of mutual expectations. John Harsanyi later added incomplete information. Reinhard Selten stripped away non-credible threats. Robert Aumann and Thomas Schelling explored the deep logic of conflict and cooperation. And Leonid Hurwicz, Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson pioneered mechanism design—the art of engineering rules to achieve social goals. Game theory had become a language for shaping the institutions of modern life.
The strategic world around us
Put on the game-theoretic lens and familiar scenes reveal new patterns. Financial markets are driven not just by fundamentals but by coordination games and the management of expectations. A central bank’s interest-rate move is a signal, read through the backward induction of every trader’s response.
The US-China trade war fuses the game of Chicken with the Prisoner’s Dilemma. Tariffs look like rational unilateral pressure but produce the collective irrationality of shared losses. Labour relations follow a Nash bargaining logic: strikes and lockouts serve as threat points, while minimum-wage laws and collective-bargaining rights are institutional moves that reset the rules.
At its core, public policy is mechanism design. Carbon markets turn emissions abatement into an incentive-compatible game. Anti-corruption oversight prevents rent-seeking from hardening into an equilibrium. The lesson is simple but profound: good institutions do not suppress self-interest—they channel it, through clever rules, toward the public good.
Robots and the race to the bottom
Artificial intelligence and humanoid robots are shaking labour markets. Game theory at first reveals a game of musical chairs: routine jobs vanish, competition among workers intensifies, capital’s bargaining power surges. If institutions stay frozen, the Nash equilibrium drifts toward an unsettling state—a race to the bottom for wages while returns to robot-owning capital become hyper-concentrated.
The way out is to redesign the rules. Universal basic income, lifelong learning accounts and robot taxes raise the “threat point” of workers, ensuring labour is not entirely powerless at the table. True symbiosis is a coordination game, not a race. We must move from the zero-sum frame of “man against machine” to the positive-sum reality of “man with machine”—where humans do the work of creativity, emotional connection and meaning-making, while machines shoulder repetitive toil.
War in the age of algorithms
Game theory has long exposed the security dilemma: every state arms for safety, producing universal insecurity—a classic multi-player Prisoner’s Dilemma. Autonomous weapons and AI amplify it dramatically.
Robot armies lower the domestic political cost of military action. The speed of autonomous systems risks triggering escalation before any human can intervene. Yet if production is already largely performed by machines, the traditional strategic value of seizing territory collapses. The losses, by contrast, could include uncontrollable global catastrophe. A rational calculus for humanity as a whole suggests that the benefits of war have shrunk far below its costs. Escaping this deadly equilibrium demands global arms-control agreements, transparency mechanisms and crisis communication channels. Otherwise, there will be no winners.
What if Marx had known game theory?
Had Karl Marx witnessed today’s AI capabilities, he might have marvelled at the leap in productive forces—then applied game theory to the systems that preoccupied his life.
Under capitalism, the model would look something like this: capitalists control AI capital, while workers supply increasingly dispensable labour. As the industrial reserve army swells, workers’ threat point approaches zero. The Nash equilibrium tilts toward extreme inequality. But this equilibrium is highly unstable. Working-class consumption power dries up, aggregate demand collapses. That is the Prisoner’s Dilemma at the heart of the automation paradox.
Marx would likely argue that socialism offers a cooperative way out. In the AI age, partially socialising the “general intellect” means of production—through taxation, public funds, social dividends and non-interest-bearing legacy bonds—could liberate labour from being a mere means of subsistence. A universal basic income would provide a floor; higher honours and esteem would still be earned through creativity and ingenuity. The game would cease to be a class antagonism and become a positive-sum arrangement among free individuals coordinating their all-round development.
On this reading, socialism is not utopia. It is an institutional design that aligns individual incentives with collective flourishing—the ultimate mechanism design, ensuring that the magnificent productive forces of our age serve to elevate everyone, not divide us further.
